title: Senters v. Savannah River Presbytery
disposition_detail: The SJC denied the procedural issue but sustained the confessional issue. It annulled Presbytery’s ruling that the candidate’s view was “not a difference” and remanded for clarification and a new judgment on that view.
first_summary: A minister challenged Presbytery’s procedures and its determination that a transfer candidate’s views on continuing tongues were not a confessional difference. The SJC found no procedural error but held that the candidate’s statements implicated WCF 1.1 and 1.6. It annulled the ruling and remanded for Presbytery to clarify and reconsider the candidate’s view.
summary: A minister challenged Presbytery’s procedures and its classification of a transfer candidate’s views on continuing tongues as “not a difference.” The SJC rejected the procedural objections because Presbytery could disregard its committee’s recommendation and had breached no required procedure. It nevertheless held that a difference need not overtly contradict the Standards and that the candidate’s statements implicated WCF 1.1 and 1.6. It annulled the classification and remanded for clarification and a new judgment, without deciding whether the clarified view would be acceptable.

sources.supports: Case identity, issues, judgment, adopted reasoning, annulment, remand, and vote.

evidence_notes.identity_and_adoption: Case No. 2022-21 and title appear at printed p. 714, lines 13–17; the amended decision was adopted 20-0, lines 25–27 and 228–231.
evidence_notes.dispute: The complaint challenged transfer-examination procedures and Presbytery’s ruling that the candidate’s tongues view was not a difference, printed pp. 714, 720; lines 21, 130–135.
evidence_notes.outcomes_and_reasons: Procedural error: no; substantive error: yes. Presbytery retained discretion over committee recommendations, while a difference need not be an overt contradiction. Printed pp. 720–725; lines 136–162, 198–226.
evidence_notes.qualifications: The SJC did not determine whether the clarified view would be semantic, acceptable, or out of accord; it required clarification and renewed judgment. Printed pp. 724–725; lines 214–226.
evidence_notes.incorporated_decisions: No decision was incorporated for its result. Jones v. Louisiana Presbytery was cited for the duty to explore an apparent difference and the definition of a difference, printed pp. 723–724; lines 192–200.

source_limits: The supplied text is the sole authority. It notes that Presbytery’s Attachment H was absent from the record (printed p. 720, line 124), but the SJC still reached a final decision.

score_reasons.concrete_dispute: Identifies both the challenged examination procedures and classification of the candidate’s view.
score_reasons.decision: States the failed procedural issue, successful substantive issue, annulment, and remand.
score_reasons.decisive_reason: Explains Presbytery’s procedural discretion and why the expressed view constituted a difference requiring judgment.
score_reasons.distinctive_value: Preserves the distinction between identifying a confessional difference and deciding whether it is acceptable.
score_reasons.fidelity: Separates the SJC’s holdings from allegations and avoids deciding the candidate’s ultimate confessional fitness.
score_reasons.economy: Retains only details needed to explain the mixed result and limited remand.

verification_notes: Rechecked the issue-level judgment, adopted 20-0 decision, and conclusion. The final summary adds the omitted limitation that the SJC did not decide whether the clarified view would ultimately be acceptable.
repair_notes: The source header labels the disposition “not_sustained” at line 3, but the operative judgment sustained the confessional issue, denied the procedural issue, annulled Presbytery’s action, and remanded. The catalog disposition should be corrected to a mixed outcome.
